Before any of it

We build the brand first, then the content.

Posting good photographs into an account with no visual rules gets you a nice-looking mess. So the first thing we do for each restaurant is settle what it actually looks like: the colours, the light, the rules a frame has to obey. Then every post after that agrees with every other one.

Neither palette below was invented. Both were sampled off your own rooms, and they are already done. This is the work, not a description of it.

A Soul Ramenone light

Your bowl already solved it. White ceramic, black type, one red dot. A warm photographic world, with black and red as the seal on top of it, never as the field. The amber is one hue at five brightnesses, which is why the room reads as a single light source. There is no cool tone anywhere in this brand.

Tang Dumplingsa lit set

Your birdcage already solved it. A red banquette inside a black timber cage, gold light along the base, one blue mural panel behind. Black builds it. Red fills it. Gold and blue only ever come from a light. Your logo red turned out to be the same red as the room, so there was nothing to reconcile.

Two restaurants, two different worlds, deliberately. A Soul is one warm light with red as punctuation. Tang is black and red with small coloured lights inside it. That is why the two feeds will never look like the same agency made them.

How this works

No shoot day. No photographer. Nothing lands on your staff.

  • Nobody gets booked.

    No studio, no set, no crew standing in your dining room through a lunch service.

  • We work from the photographs that already exist.

    Yours, and the ones your customers keep taking. A phone photo carries far more than people expect once the light and the setting are rebuilt around it.

  • Your food is never redrawn.

    The dish in the picture is the dish you serve, down to the char on the pork and the print on your bowls. What changes is the room around it.

  • You pick one of two rhythms.

    A large bank of content delivered up front, months of material at once. Or a monthly bank plus a calendar telling you which photo goes out on which day with which caption. Either way the deciding leaves your desk.

Both accounts together

The second restaurant does not cost what the first one does.

Same team, same schedule, same person to talk to, one invoice. Most of the work of starting an account happens once, so running the two together is meaningfully cheaper than running them apart.
